english: May I ask you for directions?
usage: May I ask you for directions?
존댓말 opener to any adult stranger on the street; 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다 — it lowers the speaker and honors the listener
Let me ask you for directions.
반말 to a friend or someone clearly younger; plain 물어보다 instead of humble 여쭤보다 — never use the humble form when speaking casually
May I trouble you with a question?
격식 — very formal; 겠습니다 ending lifts the level further, suited to an elder, a government clerk, or a serious setting
Excuse me, may I ask you for directions?
Softest and most natural street version; 저기요 grabs attention first and 봐도 될까요 ('would it be okay to ask') is extra courteous
examples: 저기요, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 서울역이 어느 쪽이에요?
Excuse me, may I ask for directions? Which way is Seoul Station?
Lead with 저기요 to signal a stranger before launching into your question; chaining the actual question directly is the most efficient real-life pattern
A: 죄송한데요, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 이 근처에 약국이 있나요? / B: 네, 저 골목으로 들어가시면 바로 있어요.
A: Sorry, may I ask directions? Is there a pharmacy near here? / B: Yes, go into that alley and it's right there.
Shows the complete opener-plus-question structure; B's natural answer is a direction with a landmark
실례합니다, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 제가 이 동네가 처음이라서요. 종로 쪽은 어디예요?
Excuse me, may I ask for directions? I'm new to this neighborhood. Where's Jongno?
Adding 처음이라서요 ('I'm new here') softens the interruption and invites the listener to be more patient and detailed
nuance: 직역하면 '길을 좀 여쭤볼게요' is 'I will ask you for the road a bit' — but the real function is a courteous opener before asking directions of a stranger. 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다: it lowers the speaker and elevates the listener, which is exactly right when you're asking a favor of someone you don't know. Speech level matters: with a friend or someone younger drop to the plain 물어볼게 (반말), and in a very formal setting with an elder say 말씀 좀 여쭤보겠습니다 (격식). The nearest alternative expression is 저기요, 말씀 좀 묻겠습니다, but 묻다 is neutral while 여쭤보다 actively honors the person — that humility is the real dividing line. Variant scale: 여쭤볼게요 (standard polite) → 여쭤봐도 될까요? (extra courteous, seeking permission) → 여쭤보겠습니다 (격식). The classic English-speaker mistake is launching straight into 'Where is...?' with no opener, which feels abrupt or rude; Koreans almost always cushion the question with an opener first.

structuredNuance.t: The courteous opener a stranger uses before asking directions on the street. 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다 — it lowers the speaker and elevates the listener, which is exactly right when asking a favor of someone you don't know: polite without being stiff. Use it with any adult stranger or someone socially above you; switch to plain 물어보다 with friends or juniors.

Nearest alternative: 저기요, 말씀 좀 묻겠습니다. The dividing line is humility — 묻다 is a neutral 'ask', but 여쭤보다 actively honors the listener by lowering the speaker. 묻겠습니다 is also fine but more formal and blunt; 여쭤볼게요 is warmer and more natural for a street request.

Softness scale: 물어볼게 (반말, friend) → 여쭤볼게요 (polite, stranger) → 여쭤봐도 될까요? (courteous, seeking permission) → 여쭤보겠습니다 (격식, elder/formal). The 봐도 될까요 form is especially safe when you're stopping someone who looks busy.

The classic English-speaker mistake is skipping the opener and launching straight into 시청 어디예요? — without 저기요 or 죄송한데요 first, it sounds like a demand. A second trap: trying to use 여쭤보다 when YOU are answering someone's question ('I'll 여쭤보 you the answer') — 여쭤보다 only works when you are asking UP toward the other person, never when giving information.

mistakes: Saying 물어볼게요 to a stranger thinking it's polite — 물어보다 is merely neutral; the humble 여쭤보다 is what makes asking a favor sound respectful to an adult you don't know.
Skipping the opener and going straight to 시청 어디예요? — without 저기요 or 죄송한데요 first, it reads as a command, not a request; always cushion before the question.
Using 여쭤보다 about yourself answering ('제가 여쭤봐 드릴게요' meaning 'I'll tell you') — 여쭤보다 only flows upward (YOU ask UP); it cannot mean 'I'll inform you'.

usage: 존댓말 to a passerby or station staff; point at a map, phone screen, or written address when you say 여기 so the destination is clear
반말 to a friend; identical structure, just drop the 요 — the most natural form between close people
How am I supposed to get here?
Slightly more anxious/careful tone; 가야 돼요 = 'what do I need to do to go there', useful when the route seems complicated
What do I do to get here?
Natural alternative framing; 가려면 ('in order to go') puts the purpose first, common when talking to a ticket window or information desk
examples: 여기 어떻게 가요?
How do I get here?
Said while holding up your phone map to the listener — 여기 refers to the spot on the screen, not where you're standing
A: 이 주소 여기 어떻게 가요? 걸어갈 수 있어요? / B: 좀 멀어요. 지하철 타시는 게 나아요.
A: How do I get to this address? Can I walk? / B: It's a bit far. You'd be better off taking the subway.
Showing the address makes 여기 concrete; B's natural answer gives advice about the best mode
여기 어떻게 가요? 지하철로 가는 게 나아요, 버스가 나아요? 아니면 택시가 나아요?
How do I get here? Is subway better, bus, or taxi?
Listing the options you're considering invites a specific recommendation and makes the conversation more useful
nuance: 직역하면 'Here — how do (I/you) go?' — the real function is asking the route to a destination you're pointing at on your phone map or a written address. The key insight: 여기 ('here') works because you're showing the destination visually — it refers to the spot on your screen, not where you're physically standing, so the target becomes 'here' for both speakers. Politeness lives entirely in the ending: 가요? is the everyday polite for strangers, 가? is 반말 for friends. The closest alternative expression is 여기 어떻게 찾아가요? ('how do I find my way there'), which carries the nuance of tracking down a hard-to-find spot; plain 어떻게 가요? just asks the route. Variant scale: 가요? (polite) → 가? (반말) → 가야 돼요? (polite + worried) → 가려면 어떻게 해요? (purpose-first, at info desks). The big English-speaker mistake is translating 'How can I go?' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요?, which asks whether it is POSSIBLE or PERMITTED — for directions, use 어떻게 가요? (how, by what route).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Here how do (you) go?' The real function is 'What's the route to this place?' said while showing the destination to the listener. 여기 ('here') refers to the spot on your screen or map, not your current location — the destination becomes 'here' because it is right in front of both of you.

여기 어떻게 찾아가요? adds the nuance of hunting down a hidden or confusing address ('how do I find my way there'), implying extra difficulty. Plain 어떻게 가요? just asks the route. 여기 가려면 어떻게 해요? restructures as 'what should I do to get there', natural at information desks.
Politeness is the ending alone: 가요? (polite, stranger) → 가? (반말, friend) → 가야 돼요? (polite + anxious). Combine with 버스로 or 지하철로 to specify the mode: 지하철로 어떻게 가요?

Two traps: (1) Using 거기 어떻게 가요? when you're pointing at a map — the destination in your hand is 여기 to the speaker, not 거기. (2) Translating 'How can I go?' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? — 갈 수 있어요 tests ability or permission; for route information, always use 어떻게 가요?.

mistakes: Saying 거기 어떻게 가요? while pointing at a map — when the destination is right in front of you on the screen, Koreans say 여기 because it is visually present; 거기 implies a place neither of you can see.
Using 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? for 'how can I get there' — 갈 수 있어요 asks if it is physically possible or permitted; for the route use plain 어떻게 가요?.
Dropping 어떻게 and asking 여기 가요? alone — that sounds like 'are you going here?'; you need 어떻게 to turn it into a route question.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger; 여기서 = 여기에서 ('from here'), marking the departure point of the distance measurement — this 에서 cannot be dropped
반말 to a friend; drop the 요; the meaning and structure are identical
Is it really far from here?
많이 ('a lot') signals you're worried about a long walk or ride; slightly more pressing than the bare 멀어요?
The hopeful flip side; use this when you're hoping for a short walk rather than bracing for bad news
examples: 여기서 멀어요?
Is it far from here?
The bare check you drop in right after someone names your destination — tone implies you're ready to hear the worst
A: 남대문시장 여기서 멀어요? / B: 아뇨, 걸어서 한 십 분이면 돼요.
A: Is Namdaemun Market far from here? / B: No, about ten minutes on foot.
B's natural answer gives both the verdict (아뇨) and the time estimate — the most common real-world exchange
여기서 멀어요? 멀면 택시 탈게요. 다리가 좀 아파서요.
Is it far from here? If it's far I'll take a taxi — my legs are a bit sore.
Explaining your plan (멀면 택시 탈게요) and reason (다리가 아파서) helps the listener calibrate their definition of 'far'
nuance: 직역하면 'From here, is it far?' — said to a stranger or staff right after they tell you where something is, so you can decide whether to walk or take transit. 여기서 is the contracted 여기에서 marking the starting point ('from here') — the 에서 is non-negotiable because distance is measured FROM a point, not AT it. Speech level is the ending only: 멀어요? (존댓말, stranger), 멀어? (반말, friend). The near alternative expression is 여기서 가까워요?, but it is not just a synonym — 가까워요? carries a hopeful tone ('please tell me it's nearby'), while 멀어요? braces for inconvenience; that emotional lean is the true dividing line. Variant scale: 멀어요? (neutral polite) → 많이 멀어요? (worried emphasis) → 걸어서 멀어요? (mode-specific). The English-speaker error is adding an explicit subject like 그것은 멀어요? or 그 장소는 멀어요? — Korean drops the subject entirely; the bare 여기서 멀어요? is complete and natural.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'From here is it far?' The real function is asking whether walking is realistic — you say this the moment someone tells you a location, to decide on foot vs. transit. 여기서 (= 여기에서) marks the departure point of the measurement; without 서/에서 the grammar breaks.

가까워요? is the hopeful version: you use it when you expect or hope the place is nearby, and want confirmation. 멀어요? is the cautious version: you ask it bracing for bad news. Both ask distance, but the emotional stance differs. 많이 멀어요? intensifies the worry further.
멀어요? (polite) → 멀어? (반말) → 많이 멀어요? (worried/emphasized). You can also add a mode: 걸어서 멀어요? ('far on foot?') or 지하철로 멀어요? ('far by subway?').

English speakers often add an explicit subject: 그것은 멀어요? or 그 장소는 멀어요? — grammatically possible but sounds like a textbook. Native speech drops it entirely: bare 여기서 멀어요? is complete. A second slip is 여기에 멀어요? — distance FROM a starting point requires 에서, not the destination particle 에.

mistakes: Using 여기에 멀어요? instead of 여기서 멀어요? — distance 'from' a departure point requires 에서 (contracted to 서); 에 marks a destination, not an origin.
Adding an explicit subject like 그 장소는 멀어요? — Korean drops the subject here; the bare 여기서 멀어요? is natural and complete, and adding a subject sounds foreign.
Confusing 멀어요 (far) with 모르겠어요 (I don't know) in fast speech — 멀다 conjugates cleanly to 멀어요; never say 멀라요 or 모르겠어요 when asking distance.

english: Can I get there on foot?
usage: Can I get there on foot?
존댓말 to a passerby or staff; 걸어서 = 'by walking' (걷다 + 어서, means/manner connector), 갈 수 있어요 = 'is it possible to go' — together: 'is it an option to walk there'
반말 to a friend; same structure, drop 요
Is it okay to walk there?
Shorter and very common; 도 돼요 ('is it fine/allowed') leans toward advisability rather than raw possibility — 'would it be reasonable to walk?'
Is it walkable / worth the walk?
갈 만하다 ('worth going') frames the question as a value judgment, not just feasibility; use when you want a qualitative assessment
examples: 걸어서 갈 수 있어요?
Can I get there on foot?
The bare question when you'd rather not take transit and need a quick feasibility check
A: 경복궁까지 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? / B: 네, 한 20분 걸려요. 충분히 걸어갈 만해요.
A: Can I walk all the way to Gyeongbokgung? / B: Yes, it takes about 20 minutes. It's definitely walkable.
까지 ('all the way to') marks the destination; B naturally uses 갈 만해요 to confirm it's reasonable
여기서 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? 아니면 버스 타야 돼요? 짐이 좀 있어서요.
Can I walk from here? Or do I have to take a bus? I have some luggage.
Giving a reason (짐이 있어서 = 'I have bags') helps the listener adjust their advice — the most natural street exchange
nuance: 직역하면 'By walking, is it possible to go?' — said to a passerby or staff when deciding whether to walk instead of taking transit. 걸어서 is formed from 걷다 (walk) + 어서, the manner connector meaning 'by means of', so the phrase asks 'is going by walking possible?' Speech level is the ending: 갈 수 있어요? (존댓말), 갈 수 있어? (반말). The three close variants have different focuses: 갈 수 있어요? (can I / is it possible), 걸어가도 돼요? (is it okay, advisable), 갈 만해요? (is it worth the walk, a quality judgment) — 걸어가도 돼요? is the nearest alternative expression and is very commonly heard. Variant scale: 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? → 걸어가도 돼요? → 걸어서 갈 만해요? The English-speaker trap is saying 걸을 수 있어요?, which asks whether your legs work or whether you are physically capable of walking — you need the directional compound 걸어서 가다 ('walk THERE') to ask about the route. A second mistake: 걸어서 갈게요 is a statement of intent ('I'll walk'), not a question.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'By walking can (one) go?' Real meaning: 'Is walking there a viable option?' 걸어서 is the manner connector form of 걷다 (걷다 + 어서), meaning 'by the means of walking'. This structure — verb-stem + 어서 — is essential; 걸어 alone or 걷고 would be unnatural here.

갈 수 있어요? = feasibility (can I physically/logistically go). 걸어가도 돼요? = advisability (is it okay, sensible). 갈 만해요? = worth it (is the walk reasonable / pleasant). All ask about walking but from different angles — pick by what you really want to know.
Softness/intent scale: 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? (polite question) → 걸어서 갈 수 있어? (반말) → 걸어가도 돼요? (advisability) → 걸어서 갈 만해요? (worth it). Statement of intent: 걸어서 갈게요 ('I'll walk there').

Biggest trap: 걸을 수 있어요? means 'are you/am I physically capable of walking' (as in, are my legs functional?) — NOT 'can I walk there'. You need the directional compound 걸어서 가다. A second trap: forgetting the 서 connector and writing 걸어 갈 수 있어요? — the natural form always has 걸어서.

mistakes: Saying 걸을 수 있어요? — that asks if you are physically capable of walking (are your legs okay); for 'can I walk THERE' you need the motion compound 걸어서 갈 수 있어요?.
Using 걸어서 갈게요 (a statement of intent 'I'll walk') when you mean to ask — to ask feasibility, keep the question form 갈 수 있어요?.
Forgetting 서 and saying 걸어 갈 수 있어요? — the natural manner form is 걸어서 (걷다+어서); dropping 서 sounds clipped and unnatural.

usage: 존댓말 to any knowledgeable stranger or staff; 걸리다 here means 'take (time)', not 'hang' or 'catch' — context distinguishes the senses
반말 to a friend; drop the 요; same verb
How much time does it take?
Adding 시간이 ('time') makes it unambiguous you're asking about duration, not another type of 걸리다 (to hang, to catch)
How long does it take from here?
여기서 anchors the start of the journey to your current location; add a mode — 걸어서, 지하철로 — for more precision
examples: 얼마나 걸려요?
How long does it take?
The bare follow-up right after they name a route; you need nothing else — context does the work
지하철로 얼마나 걸려요? 한 삼십 분이면 돼요?
How long by subway? About thirty minutes?
로 ('by means of') specifies the mode; guessing a number (삼십 분) invites them to confirm or correct — the most efficient real exchange
A: 걸어서 가면 얼마나 걸려요? / B: 천천히 걸어도 한 십오 분이에요.
A: How long if I walk? / B: Even at a slow pace it's about fifteen minutes.
가면 ('if I go') ties the time to a specific mode; B's answer with 천천히 걸어도 ('even walking slowly') gives a helpful worst-case estimate
nuance: 직역하면 'How much does it take?' — the verb 걸리다 has three unrelated senses (hang, catch a disease, take time), but in a transport conversation the time sense is automatic. Speech level is the ending alone: 걸려요? (존댓말), 걸려? (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 시간이 얼마나 들어요?, which uses 들다 ('go into', 'cost') and leans toward effort or resources; 걸리다 is the default for clock duration. To remove any ambiguity, add 시간이 at the front: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? Variant scale: 걸려요? (standard polite) → 얼마나 오래 걸려요? (emphasizing expected length) → 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? (explicit, formal). Combine with a mode — 지하철로, 걸어서, 버스로 — to specify exactly what kind of time you're asking about. The frequent English-speaker error is asking 얼마예요? — that means 'how much does it cost', not 'how long'; for duration the question must be 얼마나 걸려요?. Also critical: bare 얼마 걸려요? (dropping 나) sounds truncated and unnatural.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'How much does it take?' The verb 걸리다 has three senses — hang, catch (a cold), take (time) — but in a transport context the duration sense is automatic. Pairing with a mode like 지하철로 or 걸어서 further locks the meaning to clock time.

시간이 얼마나 들어요? uses 들다 ('go into / cost') and leans toward effort or resources; 걸리다 is the neutral default for travel duration. 얼마나 오래 걸려요? adds 오래 ('long') for emphasis, used when you suspect the answer is long.
Register: 걸려요? (polite) → 걸려? (반말). Add a mode: 걸어서 얼마나 걸려요? / 지하철로 얼마나 걸려요? Add 시간이 at the front for clarity: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요?

The biggest trap: 얼마예요? means 'how much does it COST' (price), not 'how long'; for duration always use 얼마나 걸려요?. Second trap: bare 얼마 걸려요? (dropping 나) sounds incomplete and awkward — 얼마나 걸려요? is the correct form.

mistakes: Asking 얼마예요? for duration — 얼마 alone asks price or money; for time you must say 얼마나 걸려요?.
Saying 얼마나 걸어요? — 걸어요 is 'walk' (걷다); the time verb is 걸리다, which conjugates to 걸려요. One character difference flips the meaning entirely.
Dropping 나 and asking 얼마 걸려요? — for 'how long' of time you need 얼마나; bare 얼마 걸려요 sounds truncated and unnatural.

english: Which exit number do I go out?
usage: 존댓말 to station staff or any rider; 몇 번 = 'what number', 출구 = 'exit', 로 marks the direction 'out through'; combine all three
반말 to a friend; drop the 요
Which exit do I have to take?
나가야 돼요 ('have to go out') is a touch more urgent or careful, used when you're not sure you'll find it
The shortest form when you need only the number — drop the verb entirely
examples: 몇 번 출구로 나가요?
Which exit do I go out?
The bare question to a station worker — pointing at nothing, relying on them to know the destination from context
롯데백화점 가려면 몇 번 출구로 나가요? 3번이요?
Which exit for Lotte Department Store? Is it number 3?
가려면 ties the exit to your destination; guessing (3번이요?) invites quick confirmation or correction
A: 시청역인데요, 몇 번 출구로 나가야 시청이 바로 나와요? / B: 5번 출구로 나가시면 바로 앞이에요.
A: I'm at City Hall Station — which exit comes out right at City Hall? / B: Take exit 5 and it's right in front.
바로 나와요 ('comes out right there') asks which exit delivers you closest; B's natural answer with 바로 앞이에요 is what staff say
nuance: 직역하면 'By what number exit do I go out?' — used at subway or train stations where each exit is labelled with a number. Speech level is the ending: 나가요? (존댓말), 나가? (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 몇 번 출구로 나오면 돼요? ('which exit do I come out of?'), heard constantly from local Seoulites; the dividing line between it and 나가요? is subtle — 나가다 focuses on the act of going out, while 나오다 focuses on arriving at the street-level result. Variant scale: 몇 번 출구로 나가요? → 몇 번 출구로 나가야 돼요? (urgent) → 몇 번 출구예요? (quickest, just the number). Combine with a destination: [장소] 가려면 몇 번 출구로 나가요? The English-speaker mistake is asking 어느 출구로 나가요? by analogy with 'which exit' — but because Seoul exits are numbered, Koreans ask 몇 번 ('what number'), not 어느 ('which of an unspecified few'). Also never use 출구에서 나가요? — the direction particle is 로, not 에서.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'By what number exit do I go out?' The real function: 'Which numbered subway exit do I use?' Seoul's subway system uses numbered exits (1번 출구, 2번, 3번…) so every local knows the system — you ask by number, not by direction.

몇 번 출구예요? asks only for the label/number. 몇 번 출구로 나가요? asks the action of exiting through it. 몇 번 출구로 나오면 돼요? ('which exit should I come out of?') is equally natural and very common. Pick 나가요? for a clear action question, 출구예요? when you're in a hurry.
Polite: 몇 번 출구로 나가요? → 몇 번 출구로 나가야 돼요? (more careful) → 몇 번 출구예요? (quickest). 반말: 몇 번 출구로 나가?. Add destination: [장소] 가려면 몇 번 출구로 나가요?

English speakers say 어느 출구로 나가요? by analogy with 'which exit' — but Korean subway exits are numbered, so 몇 번 ('what number') is the natural question word. 어느 works for an unnumbered choice between things; 몇 번 fits a numbered system. Also: never use 출구에서 나가요? — the direction particle is 로, not 에서.

mistakes: Asking 어느 출구로 나가요? — exits are numbered, so Koreans ask 몇 번 출구 ('what number exit'); 어느 fits unnumbered selections.
Using 출구에서 나가요? — exiting through a door takes the direction particle 로 (출구로); 에서 marks the location you act within, not the door you pass through.
Saying 몇 출구 without 번 — the counter 번 is required when asking about numbered items: 몇 번 출구, not 몇 출구.

english: Does this go to City Hall?
usage: Does this (bus/train) go to City Hall?
존댓말; 이거 ('this one') points at the specific vehicle in front of you — the most natural boarding check to a driver or fellow passenger
Does this go to City Hall?
반말 to a friend boarding together
Does this bus go to City Hall?
이 버스 is more specific than 이거 when there are multiple vehicles and you want to be unambiguous about which one
Does this head toward City Hall?
쪽으로 ('in the direction of') asks about general heading rather than exact stop — useful when you only need to go roughly that way
examples: 기사님, 이거 시청 가요?
Driver, does this go to City Hall?
기사님 is the respectful address term for a bus or taxi driver — always use it when speaking to the driver; it keeps the exchange polite at the door
이거 시청 가요? 시청에서 내리려고요.
Does this go to City Hall? I'm trying to get off at City Hall.
내리려고요 ('I'm intending to get off there') explains your purpose and helps the driver confirm if this is the right service
A: 이거 시청 가요? / B: 네, 가요. 세 정류장 더 가면 돼요.
A: Does this go to City Hall? / B: Yes, it does. Three more stops.
B's natural answer gives both confirmation and the count of remaining stops — the most useful reply a rider gets
nuance: 직역하면 'This one — City Hall — does it go?' — a rapid boarding check fired at a bus driver or fellow passenger as you step on or approach. 이거 ('this one') points at the exact vehicle; the destination particle 에 is dropped in casual transit speech. Speech level: address the driver as 기사님 + 이거 시청 가요? (존댓말); between friends use 이거 시청 가? (반말). The near alternative expression is 이거 시청 쪽으로 가요?, which asks for general direction ('does it head toward City Hall?') rather than 'does it actually stop there' — use it when you only need to be in that area, not at the exact stop. Variant scale: 이거 시청 가요? → 이 버스 시청 가요? (specifying the vehicle) → 이거 시청 쪽으로 가요? (direction only). The English-speaker trap is over-formalizing: 이것은 시청에 갑니까? is grammatically correct but textbook-stiff and far too slow for a doorway. A crucial wrong form is 이거 시청 와요? — from the passenger's perspective the bus 가다 ('goes') there, not 오다 ('comes').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'This one — City Hall — does it go?' The real function: a rapid boarding check asking whether this specific vehicle stops at your destination. 이거 is a very casual pronoun pointing at the vehicle; it works precisely because both speakers can see it.

이거 시청 쪽으로 가요? asks general direction ('does it head toward City Hall?') — fine when you just need to be in that area. 이거 시청 가요? asks whether it actually stops there. The first is safer if you're unsure of the exact stop; the second is sharper if you need the right stop.

존댓말 이거 시청 가요? is right for drivers (always add 기사님 first) and adult strangers. 반말 이거 시청 가? for friends. The Sino-Korean formal 이 버스가 시청에 정차하나요? is correct but sounds like a survey, not a quick boarding question.

Two traps: (1) 이거 시청 와요? — from the passenger's side the bus 가다 (goes) to the destination, not 오다 (comes); reverse the direction. (2) 이것은 시청에 갑니까? — grammatically fine but stiff and way too slow for a bus door; the clipped 이거 시청 가요? is the real form.

mistakes: Saying 이거 시청 와요? — from your viewpoint as a passenger the bus 'goes' (가다) to City Hall, not 'comes'; use 가요.
Over-formalizing as 이것은 시청에 갑니까? — correct but textbook-stiff and too slow for a doorway; real riders say 이거 시청 가요?.
Forgetting 기사님 and just barking the question at the driver — addressing them as 기사님 first keeps the interaction polite and is standard practice.

usage: 존댓말 to station staff or any knowledgeable rider; 갈아타다 = 'change vehicles', 어디서 = 'at which location' — the transfer happens AT a station, so 에서 is required
Where do I have to transfer?
갈아타야 돼요 ('have to change') conveys mild urgency — use when you're worried about missing the stop
Which line do I transfer to?
When you need the line number rather than the station name; 호선 = 'subway line', 으로 marks the direction of transfer
examples: 어디서 갈아타요?
Where do I transfer?
The bare question once you know your journey isn't direct — let the listener fill in the station name
강남 가려면 어디서 갈아타요? 신도림이요?
Where do I transfer to get to Gangnam? Sindorim?
가려면 ties the transfer to your final destination; guessing (신도림이요?) gets a faster yes/no response
A: 이 지하철 타고 가다가 어디서 갈아타야 돼요? / B: 고속터미널역에서 3호선으로 갈아타시면 돼요.
A: Riding this subway, where do I need to transfer? / B: Transfer to Line 3 at Express Terminal Station.
가다가 ('while going, then') marks a mid-journey switch; B's natural answer gives both station AND line number
nuance: 직역하면 'At where do I change-and-ride?' — asked of station staff or a knowledgeable rider when your route requires a transfer. 갈아타다 is a compound verb formed from 갈다 ('replace/change') + 타다 ('ride'); it is far more natural than the clumsy paraphrase 버스를 바꿔서 타요. The transfer happens AT a station, so the location takes 에서 (contracted to 서 in 어디서): that 에서 is non-negotiable. Speech level is the ending: 갈아타요? (존댓말), 갈아타? (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 몇 호선으로 갈아타요?, which asks which LINE to switch to (note 으로, direction toward the line), versus 어디서 갈아타요? which asks the station — pick by what information you're missing. Variant scale: 어디서 갈아타요? → 어디서 갈아타야 돼요? (urgent) → 어디서 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? (asking both). The English-speaker pitfall is building 'transfer' from two English ideas: 버스를 바꿔서 타요 sounds like you're exchanging a physical ticket; the single idiomatic verb 갈아타다 is always the right choice.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'At where do I change-and-ride?' 갈아타다 is a single compound: 갈다 (replace/swap) + 타다 (ride). The transfer is an action performed AT a station, so the location takes 에서: 어디서 (= 어디에서). This 에서 is non-negotiable; 어디에 갈아타요? is wrong.

어디서 갈아타요? asks the station (where). 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? asks the line (which line). Often you need both — 어디서 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? is a natural combined question. The 으로 in 호선으로 marks the new line as the destination of the transfer.
어디서 갈아타요? (polite) → 어디서 갈아타야 돼요? (urgent/careful) → 어디서 갈아타? (반말). Combine: 어디서 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? adds the line question in one breath.

The temptation is to build 'change buses' as two verbs: 버스를 바꿔서 타요 — sounds like you're swapping a ticket for another physical item. The correct single verb 갈아타다 is what all Koreans use. Also: do NOT say 어디에 갈아타요? — 에 marks a destination, not the location of an action; the action particle is 에서.

mistakes: Saying 어디에 갈아타요? — transferring is an action done AT a station, so it takes 에서 (어디서); 어디에 marks a destination you go to, not where you perform an action.
Translating 'change buses' literally as 버스를 바꿔서 타요 — the idiomatic single compound verb is 갈아타다; 바꾸다 sounds like swapping physical objects.
Using 에 for the new line — you transfer TO a line with 으로: 2호선으로 갈아타요, not 2호선에 갈아타요.

usage: 존댓말; both a statement and an implicit 'please step aside'; 내리다 = 'get off/down from a vehicle'; 여기서 (여기에서) marks the spot — 에서 is required, not 에
I'm getting off here. / Get off here.
반말; can be either a personal statement or telling a friend where they should alight
내릴게요 ('I'll get off') is a soft heads-up using the 게요 ending — the most considerate form for a packed bus because it warns others ahead of time
Is this where we get off?
Same words with a rising tone become a question; checking with a companion or another passenger whether this is your shared stop
examples: 잠시만요, 여기서 내릴게요. 좀 지나갈게요.
Excuse me, I'll be getting off here. Let me through.
잠시만요 (just a moment) + 내릴게요 + 지나갈게요 ('let me pass') is the full polite package on a crowded bus — three phrases, one move
A: 다음에서 내려요? / B: 아니요, 여기서 내려요. 지금이에요.
A: Are we getting off at the next stop? / B: No, we get off here — this is it.
Contrasting 다음 (next) with 여기 (here) and adding 지금이에요 ('it's now') creates real urgency — the most natural panicked exchange
기사님, 여기서 세워 주세요. 저 여기서 내려요.
Driver, please stop here. I'm getting off here.
Pairing 세워 주세요 (stop the vehicle) with 내려요 (I'll alight) is the safest combo when asking a taxi or bus driver to halt — shows the difference between the two phrases
nuance: 직역하면 'From here I get down' — 내리다 is the verb for alighting from any vehicle (bus, subway, taxi), and 여기서 (= 여기에서) marks the location of the alighting. The 에서 is non-negotiable: 내리다 takes the FROM/AT particle 에서, never the destination particle 에. Speech level shapes the nuance: 내릴게요 (using the 게 'I'll do it' ending) is the gentlest, warning fellow passengers to make room; 내려요 is a neutral polite statement; 내려 is casual (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 세워 주세요 ('please stop the vehicle'), which is directed at the driver — the dividing line is 내려요 announces YOUR own action while 세워 주세요 commands the driver's action; you often need both together. Variant scale: 내릴게요 (heads-up) → 내려요 (polite statement) → 내려 (반말) → 내려야 돼요 (urgent/forced). The English-speaker error is saying 여기서 나가요 for 'get out' — 나가다 is for exiting a building or room on foot; leaving a vehicle is always 내리다.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'From here I get down.' 내리다 is the correct verb for alighting from any vehicle — bus, subway, taxi. The point of alighting takes 에서 (여기서); using 에 (여기에) is wrong. In a crowded vehicle 여기서 내릴게요 also serves as a social signal meaning 'please make room for me'.

세워 주세요 ('please stop the vehicle') commands the driver to halt. 여기서 내려요 announces your own action of alighting. You often need both: 기사님, 여기서 세워 주세요 — 저 여기서 내려요. Using 내려요 alone to a taxi driver without 세워 주세요 means they might not know to stop.

Softness scale: 내릴게요 (heads-up, softest) → 내려요 (polite statement) → 내려 (반말). For action-oriented urgency: 지금 내려요! ('I'm getting off NOW!'). Question form (rising tone): 여기서 내려요? = 'is this where we get off?'

여기서 나가요 is wrong for 'get off a vehicle' — 나가다 means exiting a room, building, or enclosed space on foot; 내리다 is specifically for descending from / leaving a vehicle. A second trap: 여기에 내려요 with 에 instead of 에서 — the spot of alighting requires 에서.

mistakes: Saying 여기서 나가요 to mean 'I get off here' — 나가다 is exiting a room or building on foot; leaving a vehicle is always 내리다.
Using 여기에 내려요 — the spot where you alight takes 에서 (여기서), not the destination particle 에.
Telling a taxi driver only 여기서 내려요 to make them stop — that announces your action but doesn't command the driver; add 여기서 세워 주세요 to explicitly ask for a halt.

usage: 존댓말 to a fellow rider; 다음 역 = 'next station', 이 is the subject particle — natural on the subway when you've lost track
반말 to a friend; 어디예요 → 어디야
For a BUS use 정류장 ('stop/station'); 역 is for trains and subway — mixing them up marks you as a foreigner
무슨 역 specifically requests the station's NAME — use when you need the name to match a map, not just a count of stops
examples: 저기요, 다음 역이 어디예요? 제가 깜빡 졸았어요.
Excuse me, what's the next station? I dozed off.
깜빡 졸았어요 ('I nodded off briefly') is the natural explanation — it invites sympathy and a helpful answer; 저기요 respectfully grabs a fellow passenger's attention
A: 다음 역이 어디예요? 시청역 아직 멀었어요? / B: 아니요, 두 정거장만 더 가면 돼요.
A: What's the next station? Is City Hall still far? / B: No, just two more stops.
아직 멀었어요? ('still far?') asks remaining distance in stops; B's answer in stops is more useful than station names
다음이 무슨 역이에요? 제가 지도 확인하려고요.
What station is next? I want to check my map.
지도 확인하려고요 ('I want to check the map') is a natural reason; 무슨 역 frames the question as specifically needing the station name
nuance: 직역하면 'The next station — where is it?' — asked of a fellow passenger when you've drifted or lost track of the stops. The crucial vocabulary: 역 means a train or subway station; on a bus the word is 정류장. Speech level is the ending: 어디예요? (존댓말, stranger or adult), 어디야? (반말, friend). The subject particle 이 is natural (다음 역이) but freely dropped in fast speech (다음 역 어디예요?). The nearest alternative expression is 다음이 무슨 역이에요?, which specifically asks for the station NAME (matches your map), whereas 어디예요? accepts either a name or a count ('two more stops') — the dividing line is precision of identity. Variant scale: 다음 역이 어디예요? → 다음이 무슨 역이에요? (name required) → 시청역 몇 정거장 남았어요? (count). English speakers sometimes ask 다음 역은 무엇입니까? — bookish and odd, because 무엇 fits objects, not places; use 어디 or 무슨 역 for station identity.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'The next station — where is it?' Real function: asked of a nearby passenger when you've lost track of stops, or when the announcement was unclear. 역 (train/subway) and 정류장 (bus stop) are not interchangeable — using the wrong one signals you're unfamiliar with Korean transit.

다음 역이 어디예요? accepts any answer — a name, a direction, a count of stops. 다음이 무슨 역이에요? specifically requests the station NAME, useful when you need to match it to a map. 몇 정거장 남았어요? ('how many stops left?') asks count rather than identity.
Register: 다음 역이 어디예요? (polite) → 다음 역이 어디야? (반말). Add specificity: 다음이 무슨 역이에요? (name). Check distance: 시청역 몇 정거장 남았어요?

Using 역 on a bus is the most common navigation error — always switch to 정류장 for bus stops. For the question itself, 다음 역은 무엇입니까? is bookish and unnatural; 무엇 is for objects, not places — use 어디예요? or 무슨 역이에요? Also: 다른 역 ('a different station') vs. 다음 역 ('the next station') — 다른/다음 sound similar but mean very different things.

mistakes: Using 역 for a bus stop — trains and subway use 역; buses use 정류장. 다음 역 said on a bus sounds odd to every Korean.
Asking 다음 역은 무엇입니까? — 무엇 fits objects; for a station identity use 어디예요? or 무슨 역이에요?.
Confusing 다음 (next, sequential) with 다른 (another, different) — 다른 역 means 'a different station', not 'the next one'.

usage: 존댓말; practical advice given to someone deciding between transit options; 빠르다 is 르-irregular → 빨라요 (not 빠르어요)
반말 to a friend — the everyday casual form
더 ('more') makes the comparison explicit — use when the alternative has just been mentioned so the contrast is clear
At this hour the subway is faster.
이 시간엔 = '이 시간에는' ('at this time') pins the advice to current conditions, especially rush hour traffic jams
examples: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. 지금 길이 많이 막혀요.
The subway is faster than the bus — traffic's really backed up.
보다 ('than') sets up the explicit comparison; 막혀요 ('traffic is blocked') gives the practical reason — the most natural advisory form
A: 버스로 갈까요, 지하철로 갈까요? / B: 지하철이 빨라요. 이 시간엔 버스가 많이 막혀요.
A: Should we go by bus or by subway? / B: The subway's faster. Buses get stuck in traffic at this hour.
B gives a recommendation + reason — the natural two-part answer; the comparison is implied by 이 시간엔
A: 인천공항 가는 데 지하철 타는 게 나아요? / B: 네, 시간도 빠르고 가격도 싸요.
A: Is it better to take the subway to Incheon Airport? / B: Yes, it's both faster and cheaper.
빠르다 and 싸다 paired together give two reasons — shows that 빨라요 is often just one of several practical advantages
nuance: 직역하면 'The subway is fast/faster' — practical travel advice when someone is weighing transit options. 빠르다 is a 르-irregular adjective: before 아/어, the stem doubles the ㄹ to give 빨라요 (not 빠르어요). Speech level is the ending: 빨라요 (존댓말), 빨라 (반말). To set up the comparison explicitly, put the slower option + 보다 ('than') before the subject: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. The near alternative expression is 지하철이 더 나아요 ('the subway's better overall'), which folds in cost and comfort as well; 빨라요 specifically means speed only — choose it when time is what matters. Variant scale: 빨라요 → 더 빨라요 → 훨씬 빨라요 ('much faster') → 이 시간엔 빨라요 (situational). English speakers sometimes confuse 빠르다 (fast, of speed or earliness) with 이르다 (early, of time) — for an early arrival use 일찍 왔어요, not 빨라요. Also watch the particle order: 지하철은 버스가 빨라요 is garbled; put 보다 on the slower item.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'The subway is fast/faster.' Practical use: an advisory recommendation about transit choice, usually in a comparison. The 이/가 particle on 지하철이 marks it as the focus of the comparison ('it is the subway that is fast').

지하철이 더 나아요 ('the subway is better') is broader — it covers speed, cost, and comfort together. 지하철이 빨라요 is specifically about speed. If you mean 'I recommend the subway for all reasons', say 나아요; if you mean 'it's strictly quicker', say 빨라요.
르 불규칙: 빠르다 → 빨라요 / 빨라 / 빨랐어요 (past). Comparison: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. Stronger: 훨씬 빨라요 ('much faster'). Situational: 이 시간엔 / 지금은 지하철이 빨라요.

Two traps: (1) 빠르어요 — 르-irregular rules change the stem; the correct form is always 빨라요. (2) 빨라요 for 'early' — 빠르다 can mean early in some contexts (빨리 came = arrived early), but for a specific clock time 'I'm early' use 일찍 왔어요 or 이르다, not 빨라요. (3) Wrong particle order: 지하철은 버스가 빨라요 is garbled; put 보다 on the slower item — 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요.

mistakes: Conjugating it as 빠르어요 — 빠르다 is 르-irregular and becomes 빨라요 (not 빠르어요 or 빠러요).
Wrong particle placement: 지하철은 버스가 빨라요 is garbled — put 보다 on the slower option: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요.
Using 빨라요 for 'I arrived early' (clock time) — speed and earliness overlap in Korean but for 'I came early' say 일찍 왔어요; 빨라요 alone means 'it is fast'.

usage: 존댓말 to a passerby on the street; 정류장 = 'stop' for buses; often shortened to just 정류장 어디예요? in context
반말 to a friend; 어디예요 → 어디야
Where is there a bus stop?
있어요 ('is there') foregrounds existence — use when you're not sure there's one nearby and you're searching for any stop at all
Same frame, swap 정류장 → 역; useful when you're switching from bus to subway mid-journey
examples: 저기요, 가까운 버스 정류장 어디예요?
Excuse me, where's the nearest bus stop?
가까운 ('nearest') is the most natural modifier — you almost always want the CLOSEST one; 저기요 grabs attention politely
151번 타는 정류장이 어디 있어요?
Where's the stop where I catch the 151 bus?
151번 타는 ('where you board the 151') is more specific than a generic stop question; 있어요 is used because you're searching for a specific one
A: 버스 정류장 어디예요? 비 올 것 같아서요. / B: 저기 편의점 앞에 있어요.
A: Where's the bus stop? Looks like rain. / B: It's right in front of that convenience store over there.
A's reason (비 올 것 같아서요 = 'looks like rain') explains the urgency; B's natural answer uses a landmark (편의점 앞) — the most common real-world exchange
nuance: 직역하면 'Bus stop — where is it?' — a high-frequency question to a passerby when you need to find where buses load. Key vocabulary: 정류장 is 'bus stop'; 역 is a railway or subway station — they are not interchangeable, and 버스 역 is simply wrong. Speech level is the ending: 어디예요? (존댓말, stranger), 어디야? (반말, friend). In fast speech the subject particle is usually dropped: 버스 정류장 어디예요? rather than 버스 정류장이 어디예요? The nearest alternative expression is 정류장이 어디 있어요?: 어디예요? assumes the stop exists and asks its location, while 어디 있어요? foregrounds existence and fits when you're not sure there's a stop in this neighborhood — that is the true dividing line. Variant scale: 버스 정류장 어디예요? → 가까운 버스 정류장 어디예요? (nearest) → 정류장이 어디 있어요? (existence check). The English-speaker mistake is using the loanword 버스 스탑 or saying 버스 역 — neither is idiomatic; say 버스 정류장 or just 정류장.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Bus stop — where is it?' High-frequency street question. 정류장 is the only correct word for a bus stop; 역 belongs to trains and subways, and 버스 역 is ungrammatical in natural Korean. The subject particle 이 is normally dropped in street speech.

어디예요? = 'where is it?' — assumes the stop exists nearby. 어디 있어요? = 'where is there one?' — you're searching, uncertain one exists. If you've just arrived in an unfamiliar area and genuinely don't know if buses run there, use 있어요?; if you're in a normal city neighborhood, use 어디예요?.
To any adult stranger on the street: 존댓말 버스 정류장 어디예요? or 어디 있어요?. To a friend: 반말 버스 정류장 어디야?. To narrow down: add 가까운 ('nearest'), a bus number (151번 타는), or a direction (이 쪽에).

Two traps: (1) 버스 역 or 버스 스탑 — neither is standard; 버스 정류장 (or just 정류장) is always right. (2) Over-inserting the particle: 버스 정류장은 어디예요? is grammatically fine but sounds slightly formal; the bare 버스 정류장 어디예요? is what people actually say.

mistakes: Calling it 버스 역 — a 역 is a rail or subway station; a bus stop is always 정류장.
Using the English-loanword 버스 스탑 — not idiomatic Korean; say 버스 정류장 or just 정류장.
Over-inserting the topic particle: 버스 정류장은 어디예요? is correct but slightly stiff; the natural street form drops the particle entirely — 버스 정류장 어디예요?.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger when you need help; 길을 잃다 = 'lose one's way'; past tense 잃었어요 is required even though English says present 'I am lost' — Korean treats it as a completed event
반말 to a friend or on the phone with family
잃어버리다 adds 버리다 ('and it's done/gone'), stressing irreversibility and helplessness — use when you're panicked or very disoriented
I don't know where I am.
The softer, very common alternative; 어딘지 = '(I don't know) where this is'; describes confusion rather than naming the predicament directly
examples: 저기요, 길을 잃었어요. 시청역이 어느 쪽이에요?
Excuse me, I'm lost. Which way is City Hall Station?
Combine the admission (잃었어요) with a concrete question (어느 쪽이에요?) — that's the most useful street appeal; without a question they don't know how to help
A: 왜 이렇게 늦었어요? / B: 죄송해요, 길을 잃어버렸어요. 골목이 다 비슷하게 생겼어요.
A: Why are you so late? / B: Sorry, I got totally lost. All the alleys look the same.
잃어버렸어요 (emphatic, completed) fits the apology tone; the reason 골목이 다 비슷하게 생겼어요 ('all the alleys look alike') is a natural, sympathetic explanation
관광하다가 길을 잃었어요. 여기가 어딘지 모르겠어요. 지도 좀 봐도 될까요?
I got lost while sightseeing. I don't know where I am. Can I take a look at a map?
Layering both phrases (길을 잃었어요 + 어딘지 모르겠어요) makes the situation completely clear; the map request is the natural next step
nuance: 직역하면 'The road [I] have lost' — 길을 잃다 is the set idiomatic phrase for being lost, with 길 taking the object particle 을 (required, not optional). The past tense 잃었어요 is correct even though English says present 'I AM lost', because Korean treats the losing as a completed event that resulted in your current state. Speech level: 잃었어요 (존댓말), 잃었어 (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 여기가 어딘지 모르겠어요 ('I don't know where I am'), which is softer and indirect and frequently preferred — the dividing line is that 길을 잃었어요 names the predicament while 어딘지 모르겠어요 describes your inner confusion. Variant scale: 길을 잃었어요 (standard) → 길을 잃어버렸어요 (emphatic, panicked) → 완전히 길을 잃어버렸어요 (completely lost). The big English-speaker mistake is using the present tense 길을 잃어요, which sounds habitual ('I lose my way regularly'); always use the past 잃었어요 for being lost right now. A second trap: confusing 잃다 (lose) with 잊다 (forget) — 길을 잊었어요 means 'I forgot the route', not that you're lost.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'The road [I] have lost.' 길을 잃다 is a set idiomatic phrase — 길 (road/way) takes the object particle 을, and 잃다 (lose) is the verb. The past form 잃었어요 expresses a completed state: the losing happened, and you are still in the resultant lost state.

여기가 어딘지 모르겠어요 ('I don't know where I am') is softer, more indirect, and frequently preferred in everyday Korean. 길을 잃었어요 names the predicament directly; 어딘지 모르겠어요 describes the confusion. Both work, but many Koreans lean toward the indirect form.
Emphasis scale: 길을 잃었어요 (standard) → 길을 잃어버렸어요 (emphatic, panicked) → 완전히 길을 잃어버렸어요 (completely lost). 반말: 길을 잃었어 / 잃어버렸어.

The biggest mistake is using the present tense 길을 잃어요 — that sounds like a habitual action ('I lose my way all the time'). For 'I am lost right now' use past 잃었어요. Second trap: confusing 잃다 (lose) with 잊다 (forget) — 길을 잊었어요 means 'I forgot the route' (different idea, not being lost); only 잃었어요 means you're lost.

mistakes: Saying 길을 잃어요 (present tense) — Korean uses past 잃었어요 for being lost right now; the present sounds like a habit ('I lose my way regularly').
Confusing 잃다 (lose something/one's way) with 잊다 (forget) — 길을 잊었어요 would mean 'I forgot the route', not that you're lost; only 잃었어요 means you don't know where you are.
Dropping the particle: 길 잃었어요 is casual and acceptable in fast speech, but in clear or careful speech keep the full 길을 잃었어요 with the object particle 을.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger; 이 근처 = 'this vicinity'; the 이 points to where you both stand — softer than 여기서 멀어요? because you're confirming a guess, not asking from scratch
반말 to a friend; 근처예요 → 근처야
있어요 ('does it exist') stresses existence/location — use when you want to know if there's one nearby, not just where a known one is
맞아요 ('is that right?') seeks confirmation of a guess you've already made — strongest when you think you're close but aren't sure
examples: 이 근처예요? 지도에는 여기쯤 나오는데요.
Is it around here? The map shows it somewhere around here.
지도에는 여기쯤 나오는데요 ('the map shows it around here') gives the source of your guess and makes the question collaborative
편의점 이 근처에 있어요? 약이 필요해서요.
Is there a convenience store near here? I need some medicine.
있어요 asks existence; giving a reason (약이 필요해서요) often prompts a more helpful answer — natural request structure
A: 제가 찾는 호텔이 이 근처예요? 주소가 이건데요. / B: 네, 저 골목 들어가시면 바로 있어요.
A: Is the hotel I'm looking for around here? This is the address. / B: Yes, go into that alley and it's right there.
Showing the address makes the question concrete; B's landmark answer (저 골목) is the natural local response
nuance: 직역하면 'Is it this vicinity?' — used to confirm a guess that your destination is in the immediate area. 근처 is a noun meaning 'vicinity/nearby area', and 이 근처 ('this vicinity') points to where you both physically stand. Speech level is the ending: 이 근처예요? (존댓말), 이 근처야? (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 이 근처에 있어요? — 이 근처예요? asks identity ('is [the place] around here?') while 이 근처에 있어요? asks existence ('is there one here?'), and that grammar split is the true dividing line. Variant scale: 이 근처예요? → 이 근처 맞아요? (confirming a strong guess) → 이 근처에 있어요? (existence check) → 이쪽이에요? (even more casual, directional). The English-speaker error is using the adverb 가까이 as a noun — 이 가까이예요? is ungrammatical; the noun for the nearby area is 근처. A second trap: dropping 에 when asking existence — 이 근처 있어요? should be 이 근처에 있어요?; the 에 marking location of existence is required.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Is it this vicinity?' 근처 is a noun meaning 'vicinity/nearby area'. 이 근처 ('this vicinity here') is a deixis pointing to where you both stand. This is a guess-confirming question — you already think you're close and want validation, not full directions from scratch.

이 근처예요? = is [a specific known place] in this area? (identity). 이 근처에 있어요? = is there one (of a type) in this area? (existence). 이 주변이에요? uses 주변 ('surroundings'), nearly synonymous but slightly more formal and broader. 이쪽이에요? = 'is it this way?' — even more casual and directional.
이 근처예요? (standard) → 이 근처 맞아요? (confirming your strong guess) → 이 근처에 있어요? (existence). 반말: 이 근처야? / 이 근처 맞아?. Add a subject: [장소]가 이 근처예요?

가까이 is an adverb ('nearby', modifies verbs: 가까이 있어요), NOT a noun. Saying 이 가까이예요? is ungrammatical — for 'the nearby area' the noun is 근처. Second trap: dropping 에 when asking existence — 이 근처 있어요? needs to be 이 근처에 있어요?; the 에 marking location of existence is required.

mistakes: Saying 이 가까이예요? — 가까이 is an adverb ('nearby' modifying a verb, e.g. 가까이 있어요), not a noun; the noun for the nearby area is 근처.
Dropping 에 when asking existence: 이 근처 있어요? should be 이 근처에 있어요? — the 에 marking the location of existence is required.
Confusing 근처 (vicinity, nearby area) with 근래 (recently, recent times) — only 근처 means 'the area nearby'; 근래 is purely time-related.

usage: 존댓말 command; mostly something you HEAR from a local directing you; 쭉 = vivid native adverb meaning 'straight on, continuously without stopping'
반말; directing a friend or someone younger
직진 ('straight-advance', Sino-Korean) is the formal/written register — road signs, driving-test language, formal instructions; warmer 쭉 is for spoken directions
가다가 + 도세요 is the most natural way to chain 'keep going and then turn'; 으로 is required for the direction of the turn
examples: 쭉 가세요. 오른쪽에 큰 건물이 보이면 거기예요.
Go straight. When you see a big building on the right, that's it.
A landmark cue (큰 건물이 보이면) is the most natural second half of a direction — Koreans almost always add a visual landmark to 쭉 가세요
이 길로 쭉 가다가 사거리에서 왼쪽으로 도세요.
Go straight along this road, then turn left at the intersection.
가다가 ('while going, then') chains the straight section to the turn; 사거리 ('four-way intersection') + 으로 도세요 is the natural next direction step
A: 어떻게 가요? / B: 쭉 가시다가 편의점 지나면 바로 오른쪽이에요.
A: How do I get there? / B: Go straight, pass the convenience store, and it's immediately on the right.
B uses a convenience store (편의점) as the landmark — one of the most common Korean direction landmarks; 바로 오른쪽 ('immediately on the right') pins the turn
nuance: 직역하면 'Straight, go (please)' — 쭉 is a vivid native Korean adverb meaning 'straight on, continuously, all the way without detouring'. Speech level: 쭉 가세요 (존댓말 command), 쭉 가 (반말). The near alternative expression is 직진하세요, which uses the Sino-Korean 직진 (直進, 'straight-advance') — the key dividing line is register: 직진하세요 sounds like a driving exam or road sign, while 쭉 가세요 is the warm, natural spoken form for face-to-face directions. Variant scale: 쭉 가세요 (polite command) → 쭉 가다가 + [turn/landmark] (chaining two steps) → 직진하세요 (격식). To chain two direction steps, use 가다가 ('go, and then'): 쭉 가다가 사거리에서 오른쪽으로 도세요. Turns always use 으로 (direction), not 에. The English-speaker trap is translating 'go straight' as 똑바로 가세요 — 똑바로 also means 'properly/upright', so it can sound like a mild scolding ('walk properly!'); 쭉 is the neutral, safe choice. Also avoid 오른쪽에 도세요 — turns require 으로, not 에.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Go straight (continuously).' 쭉 is a native adverb conveying uninterrupted forward motion — 'all the way, without turning or stopping'. It is almost always followed by a landmark or a second direction step in real conversations.

직진하세요 uses the Sino-Korean 직진 (直進) and belongs to formal or written contexts — driving tests, road signs, formal notices. In face-to-face spoken directions, 쭉 가세요 is warmer and more natural. 똑바로 가세요 technically means 'go straight' but 똑바로 also means 'properly/upright', risking a scolding tone — avoid it for directions.
Forms: 쭉 가세요 (polite command) → 쭉 가 (반말) → 직진하세요 (격식). Chaining: 쭉 가다가 + [turn/landmark]. Turns: always 으로 도세요 (오른쪽으로 도세요 = turn right).

Two traps: (1) 똑바로 가세요 for 'go straight' — 똑바로 can mean 'properly/upright' and may sound like a mild scolding rather than a direction; use 쭉 for neutral 'straight ahead'. (2) 오른쪽에 도세요 — turns take the direction particle 으로 (오른쪽으로), not the location particle 에.

mistakes: Saying 똑바로 가세요 for 'go straight ahead' — 똑바로 can mean 'properly/upright' in Korean and may sound like a mild reprimand; for 'straight on' use 쭉 or 직진하세요.
Marking a turn with 에: 오른쪽에 도세요 is wrong; you turn 'toward' a direction with 으로 — 오른쪽으로 도세요.
Treating 쭉 as formal — it's a casual, spoken adverb; for written or formal directions (signs, official instructions) use 직진하세요.

usage: Please call a taxi for me.
존댓말 to hotel, restaurant, or shop staff; 부르다 = 'call/summon (by phone or app)', 불러 주세요 = 'please do (it) for me' — 주다 marks the favor
반말 to a friend or close companion; same structure with the 요 ending dropped
Could you possibly call me a taxi?
불러 주시겠어요? lifts the politeness further — use with senior staff, an older stranger, or when you want to be especially deferential
잡다 ('catch/grab') is for flagging down a passing cab on the street; the dividing line is 부르다 = phone/app dispatch, 잡다 = hail in real time
examples: 죄송한데요, 택시 좀 불러 주시겠어요? 공항 가야 해서 급해요.
I'm sorry to trouble you, could you call me a taxi? I need to get to the airport urgently.
죄송한데요 softens the request; 급해요 ('I'm in a hurry') gives a reason that prompts quick action — the most natural hotel-lobby request
비가 많이 와서요, 택시 좀 불러 주세요.
It's raining heavily — could you call a taxi for me?
비가 많이 와서요 ('since it's raining a lot') as the opener explains why you can't walk out and hail one yourself
A: 택시 좀 불러 주세요. / B: 어디 가시는지 말씀해 주시면 불러 드릴게요. / A: 인사동이요.
A: Please call me a taxi. / B: If you tell me where you're going I'll call one. / A: Insadong.
Shows the natural two-turn exchange at a hotel desk — staff asks destination so they can dispatch the right taxi
nuance: 직역하면 'Taxi please call (for me)' — the request you make to hotel, restaurant, or shop staff to summon a taxi by phone or app. 부르다 means 'call/summon', and adding 주세요 (from 주다, 'give') turns it into a polite favor request — that 주세요 is load-bearing; without it you're narrating, not asking. Speech level: 불러 주세요 (존댓말), 불러 줘 (반말); raise politeness to 불러 주시겠어요? for senior staff or elders. The nearest alternative expression is 택시 좀 잡아 주세요, using 잡다 ('catch/grab') — the dividing line is phone dispatch (부르다) vs. street hailing (잡다): if the staff could step outside and flag a passing cab, use 잡아 주세요; if it's an app or phone call, use 불러 주세요. Variant scale: 불러 줘 (반말) → 불러 주세요 (polite) → 불러 주시겠어요? (deferential). 부르다 is 르-irregular: it conjugates to 불러 (not 부르어), so 불러 주세요 is correct. The English-speaker mistake is omitting 주세요 and saying 택시 불러요 — that reads as a description ('someone is calling a taxi'), not a request.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Taxi please call (for me).' 부르다 means call/summon — here by phone or app. The 주세요 (please do for me) at the end is what makes this a polite request rather than a statement; removing it changes the meaning entirely.

잡아 주세요 uses 잡다 ('grab/catch') and fits hailing a cab on the street in real time. 부르다 is for dispatch — phone, hotel desk, or app. In practice today, 카카오T로 불러 주세요 ('call via Kakao T') is the most common dispatch form.
Politeness scale: 불러 줘 (반말) → 불러 주세요 (polite) → 불러 주시겠어요? (deferential). Strengthen with 좀 ('a little') for softness: 택시 좀 불러 주세요. Note 르 불규칙: 부르다 → 불러 (not 부르어).

Omitting 주세요: 택시 불러요 sounds like a third-person narration ('someone is calling a taxi') or a question ('is a taxi being called?'), not a request. 주세요 is what marks your role as the requester. Also: 부르어 주세요 is wrong — 부르다 is 르-irregular, so it conjugates to 불러 주세요.

mistakes: Saying 택시 불러요 without 주세요 — that sounds like a narration or question ('is someone calling a taxi?'); add 주세요 to make it a polite request for someone to do it for you.
Conjugating 부르다 as 부르어 주세요 — 부르다 is 르-irregular and becomes 불러 주세요.
Using 부르다 when you mean hailing a passing cab on the street — flagging down a taxi you can see is 잡아 주세요 (잡다 'catch'); 부르다 is for phoning or dispatching one.
